newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada exchanges crack down on junior miners.
newsitem.headline: Canada exchanges crack down on junior miners.

text.p: Officials at the Toronto, Vancouver and Alberta Stock Exchanges say the sizzling hot junior mining sector faces closer scrutiny after a series of wild stock market rides.
"There's no question there's increased surveillance," Neil Winchester, manager of surveillance for the Toronto Stock Exchange, said in an interview.
"We're keeping a close eye on companies that are in play. We're certainly watching them a lot more closely that we would have."
Regulators are trying to chill the junior mining sector after events set off by a pair of exploration companies traded on the Alberta Stock Exchange last spring.
Shares in Timbuktu Gold Corp have been halted since April after its stock price shot up to about 30 from just pennies on drill results from Mali.

An investigation suggested the company's ore samples were probably tampered with and that the company's then president Oliver Reese had past regulatory problems with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
In May, Cartaway Resources Corp plunged to 2 from 21 after shareholders found drill results disappointing.

Although the junior mining sector cooled down over the summer, it has heated up again this autumn and surveillance officials said they were taking extra precautions to ensure that announcements from junior companies were straightforward.

"I guess naturally every exchange is afraid of what has happened in the past with Cartaway and Timbuktu situations," said Toronto's Winchester. "That could very easily happen here. I'm not saying we're exempt from something like that."
The Toronto exchange has been using geologists to double-check news releases about material changes before they are made public, said Winchester.

Officials are also keeping an eye out for exaggerated news that may come from companies involved in Indonesia, Canada's Labrador and parts of South America that try to ride on the coattails of recent huge discoveries, he said.
Last week, the exchange halted two junior companies -- Atlanta Gold Corp and Goldstake Explorations Inc -- to take a closer look at results from Indonesia properties.

The Alberta exchange has introduced changes to restrict the involvement of brokerages in public offerings of junior mining companies. Brokerages can own only five percent of the shares under the new rules.

Vancouver officials are being more vigilant in their monitoring of directors and officers of junior companies to ensure they do not overpromote their stocks, said Angela Huxham, in charge of surveillance at the exchange.
"We've got to be like that, because with junior companies there are problems in the market," she said.

"We will look at who got shares, how much they're spending on investor relations, review all the financial statements, all new appointments of directors;, anyone new, we check them out," she said. "We're very pro-active because we've got to be. It's a long haul."
She said the exchange had kept Borneo Gold Corp halted since last week, asking for clarification of assay results from Indonesia.
But the problems of exaggerated drill results and unscrupulous promoters are no worse now than they have been in the past, said Frank Giustra, president of Yorkton Securities.
"I think the problem is there have been so many great successes - Bre-X, Diamond Fields, Arequipa," he said.
"This market is sitting on the edge of its seat hoping to find the next big one. People get overly excited and they jump the gun."
Investors buy on the slightest rumor, hoping to catch the upside of a climbing junior company. They do not take the time to study the company's prospects, Giustra said.
-- Reuters Toronto Bureau 416 941-8104
